title: Two-dimensional cellular-automaton limit sets
formal: Characterize exactly which two-dimensional subshifts are ordinary limit sets of cellular automata, allowing finitely many auxiliary states that disappear from the limit set. Equivalently, determine the realizability function \(R(q,S)\in\{0,1\}\) on the full domain of finite alphabet sizes \(q\ge1\) and subshifts \(S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,q-1\}^{\mathbb Z^2}\) defined below. Its value is 1 exactly when some cellular automaton on a finite alphabet containing those \(q\) symbols has ordinary limit set exactly \(S\), and is 0 otherwise. This is a whole-class characterization, with no computability or time requirement on the answer function.

source_formulation.text: Nevertheless, the problem of characterising which subshifts can be limit sets of CA remains open.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 1

why: A cellular automaton has a finite local description but can retain complex global configurations indefinitely. An exact realizability classification would identify which translation-invariant spatial constraints can arise in that long-term behavior. It concerns every possible initial configuration, including exceptional configurations that probabilistic descriptions may discard.
status_note: The 2015 source explicitly leaves ordinary-limit-set characterization open and proves a measure-based theorem instead. The checked later computational-invariant and generic/measure-based results do not settle the precise two-dimensional exact-realization version stated here. Bounded searches through 2026-09-16 identified no general classification; this is not an exhaustive current-openness certification.

progress.text: Borello, Cervelle and Vanier state a complete characterization of the sets of Turing degrees of one-dimensional cellular-automaton limit sets. Theorem 1 concerns computational invariants rather than exact subshift equality.

Delacourt and Hellouin de Ménibus state that ordinary limit-set realizability lacks a general characterization. Their Theorem 9 gives a two-dimensional measure-based realization result with a finite alphabet extension.
Sabrié and Törmä’s article establishes distinct ordinary, generic and measure-based limit sets for elementary cellular automaton 18; it does not claim a general exact realizability classification.

importance.reason: This seeks a structural description of all persistent configurations generated by finite local rules, linking symbolic dynamics with computation. A whole-class characterization would explain which spatial constraints can emerge from arbitrary starting configurations, beyond results describing typical behavior or only computational invariants.
importance.basis: Individual source review of the ordinary-limit-set question, the two-dimensional measure-based theorem and later work separating asymptotic notions.

sentences: A cellular automaton updates every site of an infinite grid using one finite local rule.
Its ordinary limit set contains configurations that can occur after arbitrarily many update steps from some initial configurations.
The question classifies exactly which two-dimensional subshifts can arise in this way, allowing finitely many transient auxiliary states.
The classification is represented by a realizability indicator on the full domain of subshifts, without assuming an effective decision procedure.
Results for typical initial states, computational degrees or a different notion of limit set do not determine this exact ordinary-limit-set class.

definitions: For \(q\ge1\), let \(A_q=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\). A configuration over \(A_q\) is a function \(x:\mathbb Z^2\to A_q\). Give \(A_q\) the discrete topology and the configuration space the product topology: specifying the states on any finite set of cells defines a basic open cylinder. For \(v\in\mathbb Z^2\), translation is \((\sigma_vx)(u)=x(u+v)\). A subshift \(S\) is any closed subset of \(A_q^{\mathbb Z^2}\) with \(\sigma_v(S)=S\) for every \(v\); the empty subshift is allowed. Equivalently, it is specified by the set \(\mathcal L(S)\) of all finite patterns that occur in some configuration in \(S\), where a finite pattern is a map from a finite subset of \(\mathbb Z^2\) to \(A_q\). This is an abstract mathematical domain; a subshift is not promised to have a finite forbidden-pattern description or a decidable language. To realize \(S\), one may choose any finite integer \(b\ge q\), use alphabet \(A_b\), choose any integer radius \(r\ge0\), and specify one local rule \(\phi:A_b^{[-r,r]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2}\to A_b\). The induced global map \(F:A_b^{\mathbb Z^2}\to A_b^{\mathbb Z^2}\) applies this same rule synchronously at every cell: \(F(x)(u)=\phi((x(u+v))_{v\in[-r,r]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2})\). All initial configurations in the full space \(A_b^{\mathbb Z^2}\) are allowed. Write \(F^0\) for the identity and \(F^t\) for \(t\) iterations, and define the ordinary limit set \(\Omega(F)=\bigcap_{t\ge0}F^t(A_b^{\mathbb Z^2})\). Thus \(x\in\Omega(F)\) means that for every \(t\ge0\), some initial configuration \(y_t\) satisfies \(F^t(y_t)=x\); the preimage may depend on \(t\). Identify \(S\) with its coordinatewise inclusion in \(A_b^{\mathbb Z^2}\). Define \(R(q,S)=1\) if there exist \(b\ge q,r\ge0,\phi\) with \(\Omega(F)=S\), and \(R(q,S)=0\) otherwise. Equality is exact: projecting away auxiliary states, applying a block code, matching only the occurring Turing degrees, or obtaining a superset is insufficient. No auxiliary symbol may occur in any configuration of \(\Omega(F)\). There is no bound on \(b,r\) and no uniform construction requirement across subshifts. Empty \(S\) has value 0 because every such full-space limit set is nonempty. No probability distribution on initial configurations is used.
answer_criterion: Supply a characterization, equivalently a function \(g(q,S)\in\mathbb R\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|g(q,S)-R(q,S)|\le1/100\) for every \(q\ge1\) and every subshift in the specified domain. A necessary-and-sufficient condition on the subshift or its finite-pattern language with proofs of both directions qualifies and determines \(R\) exactly. As for other function targets, merely renaming or unfolding the defining existential search over local rules and their iterated full-space images is not a determination of the function. No fixed grammar for the characterization and no computable decision procedure is prescribed. A classification only up to a factor map, only for a restricted family of subshifts, only by computational invariants, or only for a measure-based or generic limit-set notion does not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: The selected source sentence concerns ordinary limit sets, while the article’s proved characterization concerns measure-based limit sets. This card makes the two-dimensional setting of the article explicit and selects exact realization with an arbitrary finite extension of the target alphabet. These conventions are part of the reviewed version of the broad source question.

Finite auxiliary alphabets are explicitly used in the source’s realization framework. Here they may be present during the dynamics but must be entirely absent from the ordinary limit set. Exact equality is stronger than simply reading a desired component of a larger persistent configuration.

An ordinary limit set consists of configurations having preimages at every finite time depth. A measure-based limit set instead retains patterns whose occurrence probabilities do not vanish under a chosen initial distribution. The article’s Theorem 9 characterizes the latter notion for a uniform Bernoulli initial measure and does not settle the ordinary-limit-set question.

Borello, Cervelle and Vanier characterize the possible sets of Turing degrees of configurations in one-dimensional limit sets. Equal sets of computational degrees do not imply equality of subshifts, so their theorem is not an exact realization classification of the configurations requested here.

Sabrié and Törmä’s 2026 study of elementary rule 18 proves that its ordinary, generic and measure-based limit sets are distinct. This is a one-dimensional example, not a two-dimensional classification, and illustrates why the three notions cannot be substituted for one another.
